subject: Science
title: Year 9 Science Exam 4
topic: Biology · Inheritance, variation and evolution · AQA Higher
intro: Answer every question. For longer answers, write in full sentences and use key words. The 6-mark question is marked on how well you link your ideas together.

questions.q: What is a gene?
options: A section of DNA that holds the information for one characteristic
questions.ms: Answer: B. B1.

questions.q: How many chromosomes are in a human sperm cell?
questions.ms: Answer: A: 23. B1.

questions.q: Which of these shows continuous variation?
questions.ms: Answer: C: Height. B1.

questions.q: Which of these is an abiotic factor?
questions.ms: Answer: B: Light intensity. B1.

questions.q: Which type of graph should be used to show the number of students with each blood group?
questions.ms: Answer: A: Bar chart. B1. Blood group is discontinuous data.

questions.q: Describe what is meant by a species.
questions.ms: Answer: A group of organisms with many characteristics in common that can breed together to produce fertile offspring.. B1 for organisms with lots of characteristics in common / similar. B1 for can mate to produce fertile offspring (must say fertile).

questions.q:
Sort these human characteristics into inherited, environmental or both:
natural eye colour · a tattoo · body mass · blood group · a scar
questions.ms: Answer: Inherited: natural eye colour, blood group. Environmental: tattoo, scar. Both: body mass.. 3 marks for all five correct, 2 marks for four correct, 1 mark for two or three correct.

questions.q:
In pea plants, the allele for tall (T) is dominant. The allele for short (t) is recessive. Two plants that are both Tt are crossed.
Complete a Punnett square for this cross. Write the four offspring genotypes.
questions.ms: Answer: TT, Tt, Tt, tt. B1 for parent gametes T, t and T, t. B1 for offspring TT, Tt, Tt, tt.

questions.q: What percentage of the offspring would you expect to be short? (%)
questions.ms: Answer: 25%. B1 for 25% (only tt is short).

questions.q: What is the expected ratio of tall to short plants?
questions.ms: Answer: B: 3 : 1. B1.

questions.q: Using an example, describe the difference between a dominant and a recessive allele.
questions.ms: Answer: A dominant allele is expressed when only one copy is present (e.g. T for tall). A recessive allele is only expressed when two copies are present (e.g. tt gives short).. B1 dominant: shows with one copy. B1 recessive: needs two copies to show / is hidden by dominant. B1 for a correct example with genotypes.

questions.q:
Two cuttings are taken from the same plant, so they have identical DNA. One grows on a sunny windowsill and one grows in a dark cupboard. After two weeks they look very different.
Explain why.
questions.ms: Answer: Same genes, so the difference is environmental. The windowsill plant gets more light, so more photosynthesis: it grows bigger and greener. The cupboard plant is pale/yellow, tall and thin.. B1 same genes / genetic information so the difference is caused by the environment. B1 different light intensity. B1 linked effect: more light means more photosynthesis, so more growth / greener leaves.

questions.q:
Explain how a population of bacteria can become resistant to an antibiotic.
Use ideas about natural selection in your answer.
questions.ms: Answer: Level 3 answer points: variation in the bacteria; a random mutation makes some bacteria resistant; the antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria; resistant bacteria survive (less competition); they reproduce quickly and pass on the resistance gene; over many generations most of the population is resistant; overuse or not finishing a course speeds this up.. Level-marked. Level 3 (5–6): a clear, linked sequence from mutation to a resistant population over many generations, using the key words. Level 2 (3–4): most steps, some links missing. Level 1 (1–2): simple points, e.g. 'some bacteria survive the antibiotic'.

questions.q:
The Arctic fox lives in cold, snowy places.
Describe two structural adaptations and one behavioural adaptation of the Arctic fox, and explain how each one helps it survive.
questions.ms: Answer: Structural: thick fur for insulation; white fur for camouflage against snow; small ears to reduce heat loss; fur on paws for grip and warmth. Behavioural: curls up with tail over face, digs dens in snow, stores food or follows polar bears to scavenge.. B1 per correct adaptation with its explanation, up to 3 adaptations (two structural, one behavioural). B1 more for the explanations being clearly linked to survival (for example reduces heat loss, hides from prey).

questions.q:
A student wants to find out how the number of daisies changes from the shady edge of a wood out into an open field.
Describe how she could use a transect line and a quadrat to collect her data.
questions.ms: Answer: Lay a tape measure from the wood into the field. Place a quadrat at regular intervals (e.g. every 2 m). Count the daisies in each quadrat. Repeat with more transects and calculate a mean.. B1 lay a tape/transect line from the wood into the field. B1 place a quadrat at regular intervals along it. B1 count the daisies in each quadrat. B1 repeat the transect (in different places) and calculate a mean.

questions.q: Name one abiotic factor she could measure along the transect.
questions.ms: Answer: Light intensity (or soil moisture, soil pH, temperature). B1 for any abiotic factor.

questions.q:
She counted these numbers of daisies in five quadrats:
Quadrat12345
Number of daisies1215113114

Write down the anomalous result.
questions.ms: Answer: 31. B1 for 31.

questions.q: Calculate the mean number of daisies per quadrat, leaving out the anomalous result.

Only two northern white rhinos are still alive.
Give two factors that could have caused the number of rhinos to fall.
questions.ms: Answer: Any two: hunting/poaching (a new predator), habitat destruction, new diseases, more competition, changes to the environment such as climate change.. B1 each, up to 2.

questions.q: Explain how a gene bank could help stop a species becoming extinct.
questions.ms: Answer: It stores genetic material (sperm, eggs, embryos, seeds or tissue) from the species, which can be used in the future to produce new individuals or for research / breeding.. B1 stores genetic samples (e.g. sperm, eggs, seeds). B1 used later to breed / produce new individuals.

questions.q: Describe and explain two ways that people can help to maintain biodiversity.
questions.ms: Answer: Any two with explanations: breeding programmes for endangered species (increase numbers); protecting or restoring habitats / nature reserves (organisms have somewhere to live); reducing deforestation; replanting hedgerows; reducing pollution or recycling; gene banks.. B1 for each method (2). B1 for each explanation of how it helps (2).

questions.q:
Lynx eat snowshoe hares. A disease kills many of the hares.
Explain what will happen to the number of lynx, and why.
questions.ms: Answer: The lynx population falls, because there is less food so more lynx starve / fewer survive to reproduce, and there is more competition between lynx for the hares that are left.. B1 lynx numbers fall. B1 less food (fewer hares). B1 more competition / fewer survive to breed (predator and prey are interdependent).
